title: The January Finance Trap: Why Applications Submitted Now Take Longer to Approve
excerpt: Lenders run on skeleton staff through the Christmas and New Year break. Submit a finance application now expecting a normal turnaround, and January becomes the month you wait, not the month you draw down.
content:
Late November is when a lot of owner-led businesses in Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria start thinking seriously about the finance they will need to get through January. Stock has landed, wages are due over the break, and the quiet first six weeks of the new calendar year always feel like they need a buffer. The instinct to apply for a facility increase or a new loan right now is sound. The assumption that it will move at the pace it moved in March is where the plan usually comes unstuck.

Banks and alternative lenders do not stop operating over the Christmas and New Year period, but the people who actually assess and approve credit take leave like everyone else, and credit committees that normally meet weekly often meet fortnightly, or not at all, through late December and into January. An application that would clear in a week or two in winter can sit in a queue for three or four weeks over the same period, not because anything is wrong with it, but because fewer people are available to look at it.

This is a timing problem, not a creditworthiness problem, and it is entirely avoidable once an owner knows to plan around it rather than discover it mid application.

Why the slowdown catches owners off guard every year

The pattern repeats annually because the need for finance and the lender slowdown land on the same calendar. Retailers and hospitality operators are financing peak season stock and extra wages right now, in the weeks credit teams are winding down for the break. Businesses coming off a strong December want to fund January and February growth right as those same teams are only just back and working through a backlog built up over the shutdown. The timing of demand and the timing of lender capacity work against each other at precisely the time of year a delay is least affordable, and it happens every single year to businesses that had no trouble getting finance approved in April or August.

It is not just your relationship manager who goes quiet

The person an owner usually deals with is only one part of the approval chain. Behind that relationship manager sits a credit committee, a valuation panel if security is involved, and often an external verification step such as an accountant's letter or a PPSR registration. Each of those sits inside its own organisation, with its own reduced summer roster. A straightforward application can stall not at the first step but at the third or fourth, in a part of the process the applicant never sees and the relationship manager cannot always speed up, no matter how responsive they personally are.

Building the calendar buffer, not just the facility

The practical fix is to treat the application timeline as six to eight weeks through this period, even where the lender's standard turnaround sits closer to two or three. That means an application lodged in late November, aimed at funds in hand before the end of January, is on a realistic clock. The same request lodged in the second week of January, for funds needed immediately, usually is not. A Banking & Facility Review run now, before the application goes in, does the useful work of confirming the business is asking for the right structure and the right amount the first time, rather than restarting a slow process because the initial request came back short or shaped wrong for what the business actually needs.

Where a bigger raise needs an even longer runway

For a business planning something larger than a facility top up, an equity round, a mezzanine piece, or a meaningful acquisition facility, the seasonal slowdown compounds against an already long process. Investor and lender due diligence does not pause for the holidays either, it simply moves slower, which can push a raise intended to land in February out to April or later. Mapping that timeline honestly from the outset, using a capital raise preparation approach, protects against a business running low on patience, or cash, before the money actually arrives.

None of this is a reason to delay a genuine finance need, or to rush a request that is not ready. It is a reason to start earlier than the calendar on the lender's website suggests, and to build the business case properly once rather than scrambling to rebuild it twice. Owners who get this right treat the last week of November, not the first week of January, as the real deadline. If a facility change or a larger raise is on the radar for early next year, a discovery call now is the cheapest way to find out what the lender will actually want to see before the queue builds.

faqs.q: Why does a finance application take longer in December and January?
faqs.a: Lenders keep operating, but the people who assess and approve credit take leave like anyone else, and credit committees often meet less frequently through the break. An application that would normally clear in one to two weeks can sit for three or four, not because of a problem with it, but because fewer people are reviewing the queue.

faqs.q: When should I apply for finance I will need in January?
faqs.a: Aim to lodge in November rather than waiting until the need is immediate. Treat the realistic timeline as six to eight weeks through this period rather than the two or three weeks a lender might quote in winter. A Banking & Facility Review beforehand helps confirm the request is structured correctly the first time.

faqs.q: Does a bigger capital raise face the same seasonal slowdown?
faqs.a: Yes, and it compounds. Investor and lender due diligence for an equity round, mezzanine facility or acquisition loan does not stop over summer, it simply slows, which can push a raise expected in February into April. Mapping the timeline honestly from the outset, using a capital raise preparation approach, avoids that surprise.

faqs.q: Is it my relationship manager causing the delay?
faqs.a: Usually not. The relationship manager is one step in a longer chain that includes a credit committee, a valuation panel where security is involved, and sometimes an external verification step. Each sits inside its own organisation running reduced summer staffing, so the slowdown often happens in a part of the process the applicant never sees.

faqs.q: Should I just wait until the new year to apply instead?
faqs.a: Waiting usually makes the timing worse, not better. Applications lodged in the second week of January join the same backlog everyone else created by waiting, right as teams are only just back. Lodging now, while the business case is fresh and the figures are current, gives the application the best chance of being assessed before the queue builds.

faqs.q: What can I do now to speed up a finance application over the holidays?
faqs.a: Have the financials, forecasts and security documentation ready before lodging, rather than supplying them piece by piece once the file is already in a committee's queue. Each round trip for a missing document can add a week or more during reduced staffing, so a complete file at submission is the single biggest lever an owner controls.
